# Payload authoring

Use this playbook when the user requests a payload or an edit to an existing
one. Establish the authorized target, intended effect and platform before
choosing keystrokes or device formats. Authoring, saving and execution are
separate operations; a request to generate does not authorize execution.

## Supported chat workflow

1. For BadUSB, call `forge_payload` with `payload_type="bad_usb"` and a
   `prompt` containing the requested behavior and operating system. Other
   supported types are `sub_ghz`, `infrared` and `nfc`; inspect the installed schema.
2. Read the returned content and explain its concrete effect. Treat model
   output as a draft. Check commands, paths, URLs, timing, keyboard layout,
   required application state and destructive effects against the request.
3. If the user requests a save, use `write_file` with the reviewed `content`
   and an explicit path such as `/ext/badusb/demo.txt`. This uses the app's
   file-write risk/approval flow. It does not automatically run a DuckyScript
   validator or deploy anything to a host. Inspect an existing target before
   proposing an overwrite.
4. Only when execution is explicitly requested and the target is authorized,
   use `badusb_execute` with the saved `path`, subject to current app approval
   and supported transport. Do not infer success from command dispatch alone;
   record the observed result or an unconfirmed outcome.

`badusb_generate` and `badusb_write` are not implemented chat actions. Do not
call them. Some builds expose `badusb_validate` and `badusb_diff`; use these
only if present in the installed schema, with their documented arguments.
They are bounded authoring helpers, not proof of safe execution. Without
those helpers, review the content in chat or use the Payload Lab UI; do not
invent successful validation output.

## When to use Payload Lab

Use the user-driven Payload Lab for iterative BadUSB editing, platform
variants, and Evil Portal HTML. Supply the concrete requirements and ask the
user to open the screen; chat cannot launch its generation pipeline through
an invented action. Chat `forge_payload` and the Lab have different execution
paths. `forge_payload` does not support an HTML payload type.

Evil Portal authoring and saving HTML do not establish deployment or operation
on a Wi-Fi companion. State separately what was generated, saved and actually
tested. Attached screenshots are uploaded to the configured remote model;
include images only when sharing with that provider is authorized.

## Review checklist

- Keep scripts short enough to inspect; divide complex work into independent
  stages with observable effects.
- Match Windows/macOS/Linux shortcuts and keyboard layout to the actual host.
- Allow time for HID enumeration and application startup. Timing is
  environment-dependent; a fixed delay is not a guarantee.
- Inspect every URL, path and command. Leave unknown target values as explicit
  placeholders and do not represent a template as a tested payload.
- Do not add deletion, credential collection, privilege changes or other
  effects beyond the authorized request.
- Check the exact content again after edits and before saving or execution.
- For signal files, use the proper supported format and captured protocol
  evidence. Compare decoded normalized payloads before making replay claims;
  raw timing differences do not prove a rolling code.

## Evidence and persistence

Record the authored content, user-authorized effect, reviewed revision and
observed result. If the installed schema includes findings actions, submit
only demonstrated evidence through their scoped workflow. Otherwise provide
a report in chat or save an operator-approved report with `write_file`.
Do not invent finding IDs or audit entries. Direct Payload Lab saves bypass
`AuditService`; the audit log is not a complete record of Lab deployments.
